=== [CR1] ===
DEFENDER (standard reading) -- ROUND 1, OPENING

# OPENING: Christ had no human biological father

**Position.** The standard reading is that Christ was conceived in Mary by the Holy Ghost, with no human father. Joseph was husband and legal guardian, and the people only supposed him to be the father. I argue this from the 1611 KJV alone.

---

## I. Matthew's genealogy stops begetting at Joseph

**[L1] Matthew 1:2:** "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob; and Jacob begat Judas and his brethren."

**[L1] Matthew 1:16:** "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

**[L2]** The verb behind "begat" is ἐγέννησεν (egennēsen, "begat, fathered"). It runs through the whole list. In verse 16 it is not used of Joseph and Jesus. The text names Joseph as "the husband" (ἀνήρ, anēr, "husband, man") of Mary. The relative pronoun in "of whom" is ἐξ ἧς (ex hēs, "out of whom"), and it is feminine singular. It points to Mary alone, not to Joseph.

**[L4]** Matthew 1:2 sets the pattern "X begat Y", and Matthew 1:16 deliberately breaks it. The "begat" chain runs to Joseph and ends. Jesus is "born" out of the feminine "whom". The break is the evangelist's own marking of who did and did not beget.

---

## II. The stated source of the conception is the Holy Ghost, not a man

**[L1] Matthew 1:18:** "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

**[L1] Matthew 1:20:** "…fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** "Of the Holy Ghost" is ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου (ek pneumatos hagiou, "out of the Holy Spirit"). The preposition ἐκ (ek, "out of, from") marks the origin. The text says what is conceived in her comes out of the Holy Ghost.

**[L3] Luke 1:35:** "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

**[L2]** "Of thee" is ἐκ σοῦ (ek sou, "out of you"). Her alone is named as the human source. "Therefore" is διό (dio, "for which reason"). The title "Son of God" is tied to this conception.

**[L4]** Matthew 1:18 and 1:20 name the Holy Ghost as the origin ([L1] with [L2] ek). Luke 1:35 names Mary as the only human source ([L3] with [L2] ek sou). Together they leave no place for a human begetter.

---

## III. Mary was a virgin, and no man had known her

**[L1] Luke 1:34:** "Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"

**[L2]** "Know" is γινώσκω (ginōskō), used here as the Hebrew idiom for marital knowledge. "A man" is ἄνδρα (andra, "a male person, a husband"). Mary affirms that she has had no such relation with any man.

**[L3] Matthew 1:25:** "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son: and he called his name JESUS."

**[L3] Luke 1:27:** "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph…"

**[L2]** The word behind "virgin" in Luke 1:27 and Matthew 1:23 is παρθένος (parthenos, "virgin"). The same Greek ginōskō ("know") appears in Matthew 1:25 for Joseph. He did not know her until she had brought forth.

**[L3] Isaiah 7:14:** "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel."

**[L3] Matthew 1:23:** "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us."

**[L2]** The Hebrew word standing behind the KJV's "virgin" in Isaiah 7:14 is הָעַלְמָה (ha-ʿalmāh, H5959). Matthew 1:23 quotes the verse and renders it with parthenos.

**[L4]** The conception is placed before Joseph and Mary "came together" (Matthew 1:18 [L1]). Mary denies knowing any man (Luke 1:34 [L1], with [L2] ginōskō). Matthew 1:23 applies Isaiah 7:14 to this birth ([L3]). So no human male took part in the conception.

---

## IV. Joseph is the supposed father, not the begetter

**[L1] Luke 3:23:** "And Jesus himself began to be about thirty years of age, being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph."

**[L2]** "As was supposed" is ἐνομίζετο (enomizeto, "was reckoned, was thought"). It is a belief held by others. It does not state a fact about begetting.

**[L3] Matthew 1:19:** "Then Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily."

**[L3] Luke 2:48–49:** "Behold, thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing. And he said unto them, How is it that ye sought me? wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?"

**[L3] John 6:42:** "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?"

**[L4]** Luke 3:23 marks "son of Joseph" as a supposition ([L1] with [L2] enomizeto). Jesus answers Mary's "thy father" in Luke 2:49 by pointing to "my Father's business" ([L3]). The crowd's "whose father and mother we know" in John 6:42 is what people said, and Luke 3:23 labels such talk as supposition. Joseph's conduct in Matthew 1:19 is the conduct of a man who was not the father. The angel's word in Matthew 1:20 settles it for him.

---

## V. Descent from David does not require Joseph's seed

**[L1] Luke 1:32:** "…the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David."

**[L3] Luke 1:73:** "The oath which he sware to our father Abraham."

**[L2]** πατήρ (patēr, "father") is used in the New Testament of ancestors. David and Abraham are called "father" at a distance of many generations, so the word does not mean a begetter in every use.

**[L1] Romans 1:3:** "…which was made of the seed of David according to the flesh."

**[L3] Galatians 4:4:** "God sent forth his Son, made of a woman."

**[L2]** In both verses "made" is γενόμενον (genomenon, "having come to be"). In Galatians the source is ἐκ γυναικός (ek gynaikos, "out of a woman").

**[L4]** Romans 1:3 says Christ's flesh is of David's seed ([L1]). Galatians 4:4 says he came "of a woman" ([L3] with [L2] ek gynaikos). Luke 1:35 gives Mary as the only human source ([L3]). So the Davidic flesh comes through Mary. Luke 1:32 uses "father David" in the ancestral sense of Luke 1:73. Neither verse needs Joseph's seed.

---

## VI. The pattern foretold

**[L1] Hebrews 10:5:** "…a body hast thou prepared me."

**[L2]** The word for "body" is σῶμα (sōma, "body"). It is said to be "prepared", not begotten by a man.

**[L3] Genesis 3:15:** "…between thy seed and her seed."

**[L2]** "Seed" here is זֶרַע (zeraʿ, "seed"). It is attributed to "her", the woman, not to a man.

**[L4]** Genesis 3:15 ([L3] with [L2] zeraʿ) speaks of the woman's seed. Hebrews 10:5 ([L1] with [L2] sōma) speaks of a body prepared for him. Both fit the Gospel account of a birth without a human father.

---

## DECLARED CHAIN

1. Matthew's genealogy breaks the "begat" pattern at Joseph and uses the feminine "of whom" for Jesus. Footing: [L1] Matthew 1:2 and Matthew 1:16; [L2] egennēsen ("begat") and ex hēs ("out of whom", feminine). Chain: the verb runs to Joseph and stops, and the birth is traced out of Mary alone.
2. The source of the conception is the Holy Ghost, and Mary is the only human source. Footing: [L1] Matthew 1:20 "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost"; [L2] ek pneumatos hagiou ("out of the Holy Spirit"); [L3] Luke 1:35 with ek sou ("out of you"). Chain: one source is named from above and one from below, and a human begetter is not named.
3. Mary was a virgin and had known no man before the conception. Footing: [L1] Luke 1:34 "seeing I know not a man"; [L2] ginōskō ("know") and parthenos ("virgin"); [L3] Matthew 1:25 and Isaiah 7:14 with Matthew 1:23. Chain: Mary's own statement, the "virgin" of the prophecy, and Joseph's not knowing her until she had brought forth all agree.
4. Joseph was the supposed father and not the begetter. Footing: [L1] Luke 3:23 "as was supposed"; [L2] enomizeto ("was reckoned"); [L3] Luke 2:49 and Matthew 1:19. Chain: the title "son of Joseph" is marked as a supposition, and Jesus himself names another Father.
5. Descent from David runs through Mary's flesh and does not need Joseph's seed. Footing: [L1] Romans 1:3 "made of the seed of David according to the flesh"; [L2] genomenon ek gynaikos ("made out of a woman"); [L3] Galatians 4:4, Luke 1:35 and Luke 1:73. Chain: the flesh is from the woman, so the Davidic seed comes through her, and "father David" is ancestral usage.
6. Christ had no human biological father. His conception in Mary was of the Holy Ghost, with no man having known her. Footing: [L1] Matthew 1:18 and Matthew 1:20; [L2] ek pneumatos hagiou; [L3] Luke 1:34–35 and Matthew 1:16, with links 1 to 5. Chain: the origin is stated, the human source is Mary alone, no man is named as begetter, and the supposition of Joseph's fatherhood is marked as supposition.

=== [CR2] ===
DEFENDER (standard reading) -- ROUND 2, RESPONSE

# DEFENDER, ROUND 2

I answer the challenger's question first, then C1 to C3, then the link round on D1 to D6, quoting each pressed verse.

---

## A. The question: how is it evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda?

**[L1] Hebrews 7:14:** "For [it is] evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda; of which tribe Moses spake nothing concerning priesthood."

**[L1] Romans 1:3:** "which was made of the seed of David according to the flesh."
**[L1] Luke 1:35:** "that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."
**[L3] Galatians 4:4:** "God sent forth his Son, made of a woman."
**[L3] Hebrews 2:16:** "he took on [him] the seed of Abraham."

**[L2]** Romans 1:3 and Luke 1:35 say the flesh is "of David's seed" and is "born of thee" (ek sou, "out of you"), and Galatians 4:4 says "made of a woman" (ek gynaikos, "out of a woman"). The flesh of David's seed is the flesh born out of Mary.

**[L4]** The flesh is of David's seed (Romans 1:3 [L1]). The flesh is born out of Mary (Luke 1:35 [L1] with ek sou [L2]; Galatians 4:4 [L3]). Therefore Mary is of David's seed. The descent is evident in her.

**Mary's kin.** The challenger presses Luke 1:36 (syngenēs, "relative by blood") with Luke 1:5 ("of the daughters of Aaron") to show Mary is not Davidic.

**[L1] Luke 1:36:** "thy cousin Elisabeth."
**[L3] 2 Chronicles 22:11:** "Jehoshabeath, the daughter of king Jehoram, the wife of Jehoiada the priest."

A king's daughter of David's line was the wife of a priest. Aaronic and Davidic kinship is therefore attested in the record, and kinship with Elisabeth does not exclude Mary's Davidic descent. This [L4] rests on Luke 1:36 and Luke 1:5, joined to 2 Chronicles 22:11.

**The legal house.** The challenger presses Numbers 1:18, "by the house of their fathers". A house can receive a child by taking, naming and rearing, with no begetting.

**[L3] Esther 2:7:** "whom Mordecai, when her father and mother were dead, took for his own daughter."
**[L3] Ruth 4:17:** "There is a son born to Naomi; and they called his name Obed."

**[L1] Matthew 1:20:** "Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife."
**[L1] Matthew 1:25:** "he called his name JESUS."

**[L2]** "To take unto thee" is paralambanō ("to receive near, associate with oneself", Matthew 1:20). The cited verses give a receiving and a naming.

**[L4]** Joseph, who is of David's house (Matthew 1:20 [L1]), receives Mary and names the child (Matthew 1:25 [L1]). Esther 2:7 and Ruth 4:17 [L3] show that this reckons a child into a house without begetting. So Joseph carries the house and legal descent, and Mary carries the flesh.

---

## B. Answers to C1 to C3

**C1 (seed and loins).**

**[L1] 2 Samuel 7:12:** "thy seed after thee, which shall proceed out of thy bowels."
**[L3] Hebrews 7:10:** "For he was yet in the loins of his father, when Melchisedec met him."
**[L3] Galatians 3:29:** "if ye be Christ's, then are ye Abraham's seed."

**[L2]** "Seed" in Romans 1:3 is sperma (G4690, "seed, offspring"). In Galatians 3:29 the same word names descendants who are not begotten of Abraham's body by a named line. In Hebrews 7:10 "loins" (osphys) covers Levi, generations after Abraham.

**[L4]** "Seed" and "loins" are terms of descent at any distance (Hebrews 7:10 [L3]; sperma [L2]; Galatians 3:29 [L3]). They do not require a father-to-son link at the last step. Romans 1:3 and Acts 2:30 are met by the descent of the flesh through Mary, as in section A.

**C2** is answered in section A.

**C3 (Genesis 4:1).**

**[L1] Genesis 4:1:** "And Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived, and bare Cain."

I grant that this is the ordinary means. The Gospel gives the order of events for this child.

**[L1] Matthew 1:18:** "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** "Came together" is synerchomai (G4905, "to cohabit conjugally"). "Found" is heurethē, and "with child" is en gastri echousa ("having in the womb").

**[L1] Matthew 1:25:** "knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."
**[L3] Matthew 1:24:** "took unto him his wife."

**[L4]** The order in Matthew is as follows. The child is found in her womb before conjugal cohabitation (Matthew 1:18 [L1], synerchomai [L2]). Joseph then takes her (Matthew 1:24 [L3]). Then "knew her not till" the birth (Matthew 1:25 [L1]). Every stated stage puts the child's presence before any knowing by Joseph. The "till" of heōs hou runs from the taking to the birth. It does not place a knowing before the finding.

---

## C. LINK ROUND

**LINK 1: SUPPORTED, with one concession.**
I concede that "born of" (ex hēs) alone does not exclude a father.

**[L1] Matthew 11:11:** "Among them that are born of women there hath not risen a greater than John the Baptist."
**[L3] Luke 1:13:** "thy wife Elisabeth shall bear thee a son."

D1's footing is the verse that follows the genealogy.

**[L1] Matthew 1:16:** "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus."
**[L1] Matthew 1:18:** "Now the birth of Jesus Christ was on this wise."

**[L2]** The word for "birth" in Matthew 1:18 is génnēsis (G1083, "birth, origin"), the noun of the verb gennaō ("beget") that runs through Matthew 1:2 to 1:16.

**[L4]** Matthew 1:18 opens "the birth of Jesus Christ was on this wise" and goes on to give its origin: "of the Holy Ghost." It sits directly after Matthew 1:16 (Matthew 1:16 [L1], génnēsis [L2], Matthew 1:2 [L3]). So the genealogy's last clause is explained by the origin the next verse states. D1 does not stand alone. It stands with D2.

**LINK 2: SUPPORTED.**
Pressed: Matthew 1:20, "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost. [conceived: Gr. begotten]". 1 John 5:1, "Whosoever believeth that Jesus is the Christ is born of God". John 3:6, "that which is born of the Spirit is spirit". John 1:13, "born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God". Luke 1:35 with "therefore also". Luke 1:32. Acts 1:8, "the Holy Ghost is come upon you". Luke 9:34, "there came a cloud, and overshadowed them". 1 Chronicles 28:6, "I have chosen him [to be] my son, and I will be his father."

**Answer on the believers' birth (1 John 5:1; John 1:13; John 3:6).**

**[L1] John 1:13:** "Which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God."
**[L3] John 3:6:** "That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit."

**[L2]** John 3:6 sets two births against each other: gennaō "of the flesh" and gennaō "of the Spirit". John 1:13 excludes "blood" (haima), "the will of the flesh" and "the will of man" as the source of the believers' second birth.

**[L4]** For believers, the birth of the Spirit follows a birth of the flesh (John 3:6 [L3]). For this child, the thing "conceived in her" is the one conception, and its source is stated as the Holy Ghost (Matthew 1:20 [L1]). In Matthew 1:18 that conception is found "with child" in the womb before conjugal cohabitation ([L1], synerchomai [L2]). The believers' second birth does not parallel a womb-conception found before any cohabiting. So Matthew 1:20 states the source of the conception itself, and John 1:13 does not turn it into covenant language.

**Answer on Luke 1:35.**

**[L1] Luke 1:35:** "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

**[L2]** "Therefore" is dio kai ("for which reason also"). It follows immediately the two clauses about the Holy Ghost coming upon her and the power overshadowing her. Its antecedent is in the same verse.

**[L3] Luke 1:34:** "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"

**[L2]** "Seeing" is epei ("since"). The "this" of her question is the conceiving of Luke 1:31, "thou shalt conceive in thy womb".

**[L4]** Mary's "how" asks for the means of conception, given her state (Luke 1:34 [L3], epei [L2]). The angel's answer names the means: the Holy Ghost coming upon her and the power overshadowing her (Luke 1:35 [L1]). The "therefore" ties the title to that means, not only to Luke 1:32.

**On Solomon (1 Chronicles 28:6).** There the text says "I have chosen him [to be] my son". That is choice of a begotten son, and no coming of the Holy Ghost on his mother accounts for his conception. Luke 1:35 has a stated means and a "therefore". These two do not match.

**On Acts 1:8 and Luke 9:34.** I accept that these verbs elsewhere speak of power and presence. In Luke 1:35 they stand in the answer to a question about conceiving in the womb (Luke 1:31, 34). The context fixes their use, and it is the same context that has Matthew 1:18 finding the child in the womb before cohabitation.

**LINK 3: SUPPORTED, narrowed.**
I narrow D3 to what its rows carry. Mary's "I know not a man" (Luke 1:34) is her state at the angel's word. The conception that follows is stated to be by the Holy Ghost (Luke 1:35). No knowing is placed between the angel's word and the finding. Matthew 1:18 puts the finding before cohabitation, and Matthew 1:25 says "knew her not till she had brought forth".

Pressed: Luke 1:31, "thou shalt conceive in thy womb". Luke 1:27, "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph". Isaiah 7:14, "a virgin shall conceive". Matthew 1:24 and 1:25.

**[L1] Matthew 1:23:** "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son."
**[L2]** "With child" translates hareh (H2030, "pregnant"), the adjective of Isaiah 7:14, and parthenos (G3933, "virgin") is the word for "virgin" in Matthew 1:23. The prophecy names her "a virgin" in the clause in which she is "with child".

**[L4]** The conception foretold in Luke 1:31 is by the Holy Ghost (Luke 1:35 [L1]). The prophecy applied in Matthew 1:23 gives the same woman the title "virgin" while "with child" (hareh [L2]). Matthew 1:24 places the taking after the finding. No row puts a knowing in the interval. D3 stands as narrowed.

**LINK 4: SUPPORTED.**

Pressed: Matthew 1:19, "being a just [man], and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily". Matthew 1:20. 2 Samuel 7:14, "I will be his father". Matthew 1:21, "thou shalt call his name JESUS". Luke 1:13. Acts 16:13. Luke 2:48. Luke 2:41. John 1:45. 1 Chronicles 28:6.

**On Matthew 1:19, meeting the meaning pressed.** The challenger holds that Joseph feared to take a wife whose child God claimed. The verse gives two stated grounds, "being a just [man]" and "not willing to make her a publick example".

**[L2]** "To make a publick example" is paradeigmatizō ("to make a public show of, to expose"). "Minded" is eboulēthē ("purposed").

**[L3] Deuteronomy 22:24:** "the damsel, because she cried not, [being] in the city; and the man, because he hath humbled his neighbour's wife: so thou shalt put away evil from among you."

**[L4]** A public example (Matthew 1:19 [L1], paradeigmatizō [L2]) is an exposure for a charge. In the law the charge falls on a betrothed wife and a man who "humbled his neighbour's wife" (Deuteronomy 22:24 [L3]). Joseph's mercy is "not willing to make her a publick example", and his purpose is a private putting away. A man who knew himself the father had no such charge to be merciful about. Fear of a child God claimed would not be a ground for sparing her publicity.

The angel then answers with the source: "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost" (Matthew 1:20 [L1]). That is the answer to a supposed wrong and the removal of Joseph's reason for putting her away.

**On naming (Matthew 1:21; Luke 1:13).** "Thou shalt call his name" is an act of naming. Ruth 4:17 [L3] has others name a son "born to Naomi" who was not Naomi's by bearing. Matthew 1:25 [L1] says "he called his name JESUS". So naming shows Joseph's receiving of the child and does not decide begetting.

**On 2 Samuel 7:14.** "I will be his father" (2 Samuel 7:14 [L1]) sits in a promise about David's son. It also says "he shall be my son". It states God's fatherhood. It does not state that no human father existed for Solomon, and for this child Luke 1:35 gives the Holy Ghost as the means.

**On Luke 3:23.**

**[L1] Luke 3:23:** "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph."

**[L2]** The Greek verb is enomizeto, from nomizō (G3543, "to reckon, to suppose"). The same verb, rendered "supposing", appears in:

**[L3] Acts 14:19:** "supposing he had been dead."
**[L3] Acts 16:27:** "supposing that the prisoners had been fled."

**[L4]** In Acts 14:19 and 16:27 [L3] nomizō carries a supposition that proved false. The KJV renders it in Luke 3:23 [L1] as a parenthesis, "(as was supposed)". It sets the people's reckoning of "son of Joseph" against the stated origin in Luke 1:35. The challenger's Acts 16:13, "prayer was wont to be made", is the same verb in the sense of what was thought or supposed to be the custom there. It does not show that the supposition is true.

**On "thy father" and "parents" (Luke 2:48; 2:41; John 1:45).** Mary says "thy father and I" (Luke 2:48 [L1]). That is the term used of the husband in the house, and Joseph is the one who received the child and named him (Matthew 1:24, 25 [L3]). Jesus's answer is:

**[L1] Luke 2:49:** "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?"

**[L4]** He answers "thy father" (Luke 2:48 [L3]) with "my Father's" (Luke 2:49 [L1]), and places the Father in the temple. The Solomon parallel does not fit, because David speaks of "Solomon thy son" and God says "my son" about the same man. In Luke 2:48 and 2:49 the two fatherhoods are contrasted in one exchange. John 1:45 is Philip's reckoning, and John 6:42 [L1] is the crowd's "whose father and mother we know", which is the very reckoning Luke 3:23 marks as supposition.

**LINK 5: SUPPORTED.**
Pressed: Luke 1:27, "of the house of David". Luke 1:36. Luke 1:5. Galatians 4:4. Job 14:1, "Man [that is] born of a woman". Genesis 4:25, "hath appointed me another seed". Hebrews 2:14, 2:16, 2:17.

I grant that "of the house of David" in Luke 1:27 follows Joseph, and that Joseph has the house (Luke 2:4 [L3]). The footing for D5 is section A. Romans 1:3 says "of the seed of David according to the flesh". Luke 1:35 and Galatians 4:4 place the flesh "of thee" and "of a woman". Hebrews 2:14 says "he also himself likewise took part of the same" flesh and blood, which is the flesh carried by the mother. Hebrews 2:16 says "he took on [him] the seed of Abraham". Therefore Mary is of the seed of David, and 2 Chronicles 22:11 meets the Aaronic kinship of Luke 1:36.
